w: The first basilica here went up in the 5th century over the tomb of Saint Martin of Tours, and by the 790s its abbot was Alcuin, adviser to Charlemagne himself. The medieval church was demolished in the Revolution; what stands today is a Neo-Byzantine rebuild finished in 1925 on part of the original site.
s: A pilgrim's tomb once run by Charlemagne's own adviser
_facts: Catholic basilica over the tomb of Saint Martin of Tours, first consecrated 471
Abbot of Saint Martin between 796-804 was Alcuin, adviser to Charlemagne
Medieval basilica demolished in the French Revolution; present Neo-Byzantine church built 1886-1924, dedicated 1925

w: Built in the 1st century when Tours was still Caesarodunum, this amphitheatre was raised mostly from packed earth rather than masonry - spectators sat directly on the grassy slopes. Expanded in the 2nd century to roughly 156 by 134 metres, it briefly ranked among the ten largest structures anywhere in the Roman Empire.
s: An earthwork arena once among Rome's ten biggest
_facts: Roman amphitheatre (Caesarodunum amphitheatre) built in the 1st century, behind Tours Cathedral
Built mostly of earth rather than masonry, classified as a 'primitive' amphitheatre
Expanded in the 2nd century to c.156m x 134m, among the ten largest structures in the Roman Empire; later fortified

w: Housed since 1910 in the old bishop's palace beside the Cathedral of St Gatien, this museum holds one of France's richest and most varied painting collections. The setting is half the draw - a palace built for the diocese, repurposed for art right where the bishops once ran their affairs.
s: Fine art inside a former bishop's palace
_facts: Museum of Fine Arts of Tours, located in the former bishop's palace near Cathedral St Gatien since 1910
Painting collection considered one of the first in France for quality and diversity

w: Built between 1765 and 1778, this fifteen-arch bridge stretches 434 metres across the Loire and is officially named for Woodrow Wilson - though locals still call it Pont de Pierre, the stone bridge. It replaced a crumbling 11th-century predecessor and remains the oldest bridge standing in Tours.
s: Tours' oldest bridge, still known by its old nickname
_facts: Oldest bridge in Tours, built 1765-1778, 15 arches, 434 metres across the Loire
Officially named Wilson Bridge, locally called Pont de Pierre (Stone Bridge)
Replaced the deteriorating 11th-century Pont d'Eudes; listed historic monument

w: Founded as a Benedictine house back in the 6th century, Saint-Julien's surviving buildings actually date from the 10th to the 16th century, each phase of construction now protected as a historic monument. Few sites in Tours let you walk through a thousand years of continuous religious life in one visit.
s: A Benedictine abbey with buildings spanning five centuries
_facts: Ancient Benedictine abbey in Tours dating back to the 6th century
Surviving buildings date from the 10th to 16th centuries, all classified or listed as historic monuments
